content: These efforts should include identifying at-risk groups, conducting cost-effectiveness studies, and other relevant analyses. Regarding tuberculosis (TB)-associated disabilities, there is a need for evidence to better define the populations at risk, the determinants of these disabilities, the types of care required, and the outcomes for individuals after completing TB treatment. This includes areas such as palliative care, social or psychological support, and pulmonary rehabilitation. Given the existing evidence gaps, participants suggested conducting situational assessments and prioritizing research needs to inform global TB policymaking. Randomized trials could provide high-quality evidence for policy development, while other studies are needed to improve understanding of predictors of chronic disease following TB treatment. In the interim, WHO was advised to explore the development of interim guidance to assist countries in preventing TB-associated disabilities. Dennis Falzon from the WHO Global TB Programme presented on the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on TB services. He addressed frequently asked questions about the co-management of TB and COVID-19 and described WHO/GTB’s efforts to support national TB programmes during the pandemic. These efforts included monitoring the impact of COVID-19 responses on TB notifications (on a monthly basis), issuing guidance on maintaining TB services during the pandemic, and sharing case studies of programmatic innovations to address emerging challenges in TB prevention and care. Additionally, an ongoing review of evidence on the association between SARS-CoV-2 infection and TB disease with unfavorable treatment outcomes was presented. Participants welcomed WHO/GTB’s actions on TB and COVID-19 and discussed whether guidance would be issued to prevent drug-drug interactions between Paxlovid and TB regimens containing rifamycin or bedaquiline. In conclusion, participants emphasized the importance of prioritizing research gaps relevant to policy that are repeatedly identified in these meetings and finding ways to support their implementation. Such research should include individuals of all age groups and address vulnerabilities, while also considering the acceptability, feasibility, and equity impacts of interventions, as well as gender and human rights issues. The post-pandemic context makes these considerations even more critical. Where evidence in guidelines is of low certainty, WHO was encouraged to advocate for research implementation to strengthen recommendations. In the meantime, generalized evidence synthesis using both trial and non-trial data may help address evidence gaps. Participants also highlighted the value of infographics to simplify the presentation of guidelines and facilitate knowledge sharing. Tereza Kasaeva and Matteo Zignol thanked the participants and reiterated WHO’s commitment to convening regular forums to share WHO/GTB policy development plans. The meeting concluded at 16:50.
